blogs.title: Optimizing Kubernetes admission control: Where Kyverno’s CEL admission cost actually goes
blogs.content: Posted on November 18, 2026 by Raunak Madan (Software Engineer Intern, Nirmata) CNCF projects highlighted in this post Kyverno’s CEL (Common Expression Language)-based engines exist to evaluate policy expressions. So when we profiled the admission path, we expected to find the bulk of the cost in CEL evaluation. It was not there. About 86% of what the engine allocated went into preparing the object for evaluation, and almost none of it into evaluating policy. We went looking because a public benchmark put Kyverno behind the alternatives. Those benchmarks measured the legacy ClusterPolicy JMESPath engine, which did have a real regression at the time, and the usual answer was to point people at the newer CEL-based engine instead. That answer was right but incomplete: we had not checked what the CEL engine itself was spending its time on. This post is about where that performance cost came from, why it grew with the number of policies you deploy, and what removing it did. The fix ships in Kyverno 1.19.2. Please read the limitations section before you quote any number here. And as always, run your own tests in your environments, for real-world accuracy. What the profile showed Kyverno’s CEL engines evaluate policies against a CEL activation: a set of variables your policy expressions can reference. One of those variables is request , the AdmissionRequest the API server sent, converted into the unstructured map form CEL understands. Here is a heap profile of the ValidatingPolicy engine handling admission requests, before and after the change, by share of total allocated bytes: Before, ConvertObjectToUnstructured accounted for 86.8% of everything the engine allocated. CEL evaluation itself barely registered. After, object conversion falls to 2.9%, and the largest single frame becomes evaluateWithData — the code that actually runs your policy expressions. The same pattern shows up in the MutatingPolicy engine, which was paying a smaller but still substantial version of the same cost: One caveat on reading those profiles: the post-fix benchmark completes more iterations in the same time because it is faster, so the two profiles have different absolute totals. Compare the shares, not the raw bytes. Per-request figures come from the benchmark table further down. Why: the same object, converted once per policy The API server sends the admitted object as raw JSON bytes. CEL cannot read bytes, so Kyverno parses them into the map form CEL understands before it can evaluate anything against them. That conversion happened inside the loop over matched policies rather than before it. With the Pod Security Standards set, roughly 16 policies match a typical Pod creation — so Kyverno parsed the same Pod 16 times, same input, same output, every time. The cost grew with your policy count and with the size of the object being admitted: O(policies) , where it should have been O(1). The object does not change between policies. There was never a reason to convert it more than once. The fix: convert once per request The change moves the conversion out of the per-policy loop. Kyverno builds the CEL request value once, before the loop starts, and every matched policy reuses it. Doing that without changing what policies see takes some care. The expensive part of the conversion is the admitted object itself, so Kyverno converts a copy of the request with that object temporarily blanked out — which leaves only cheap fields to walk — and splices the object back in afterwards. The same conversion code still produces the result, so the output matches what policies saw before rather than being a reimplementation that someone has to keep in sync by hand. Keeping policy behavior identical The first attempt used a single shared builder for every CEL engine. Testing caught that this quietly changed how policies behave, because the engines had never agreed on what request.object meant in the first place. Validating and generating policies saw the object exactly as the API server sent it. Mutating policies saw a normalized version. The two also disagreed about what an empty object looks like to CEL, which matters for operations like DELETE where one side is absent. Unifying them would have changed the result of expressions people already have deployed. That is a conversation worth having, but not one a performance fix should start on its own. So each engine keeps the contract it already had, sharing one fast implementation underneath. Equivalence tests pin this down: they run the original code as the reference and compare its output against the new one field by field, across every request type, so any drift fails the build. What changed The benchmark calls the engine directly with a roughly 50 KB Pod and a varying number of matched policies. It times the engine alone — building the request value, matching, and evaluating CEL. It does not include the webhook round trip, the API server, or etcd, so these are not end-to-end admission latencies. Matched policies Allocations before Allocations after Engine time before Engine time after 1 2,327 854 0.31 ms 0.10 ms 16 37,055 2,718 4.91 ms 0.16 ms 64 148,131 8,672 20.01 ms 0.36 ms The MutatingPolicy engine improves on the same curve, from 258,943 to 52,689 allocations and 10.59 ms to 2.97 ms at 64 policies. The slope is the point, not the headline multiple. Before the change, allocations grew about 63 times going from 1 policy to 64. After, about 10 times — and that residual growth is CEL evaluation, which is the work you deployed the policies to get. Object preparation is now constant per request instead of proportional to how many policies you run. Practically: adding policies to a Kyverno deployment used to carry a hidden per-policy serialization cost on top of the evaluation you asked for. It no longer does. Image verification too The image verification engine had the same pattern, with its own private copy of the conversion code, so it got the same fix. The gain there is memory rather than speed: image verification spends most of its time fetching signatures and attestations over the network, and that part does not change. How this compares to native admission policies With the per-policy tax gone, it is worth asking where Kyverno’s CEL engine actually sits against the API server’s own ValidatingAdmissionPolicy. Running the same 16 Pod Security Standards policies through both engines on one cluster, the answer depends on how many policies you enforce: At one policy, native is ahead: about 9.2 ms against Kyverno’s 12.8 ms. At the full 16-policy set, Kyverno is ahead: about 20 ms against native’s 29 ms. Those numbers were measured on Kyverno 1.19.0, which predates the change described above. The Kyverno side of that chart should now be better than shown; we have not re-run the comparison. The two engines pay their costs differently. Native dispatches each policy separately on the API server, so its cost grows with the number of policies you enforce. Kyverno pays once per request to receive the object over a webhook, and that cost is shared across however many policies then evaluate. With only a policy or two, native is ahead. Once you are running a realistic set, Kyverno matches it and can come out ahead. That framing only became accurate with this fix. Kyverno’s cost was not fixed per request before it — it was per policy, which is exactly why the curve looked the way it did. The CPU side is more one-sided. Under matched load, Kyverno’s engine used about 3.2 cores against the API server’s 8.2 for native. The surprise in the API server profile is that 67% of its CPU sits in the policy dispatch machinery while the actual CEL bytecode execution is about 5.5% — the cost is dispatching 16 policies and building an input for each, not evaluating them. And that load lands on the control plane, which you cannot scale horizontally the way you can scale a Kyverno deployment. Both numbers come from a si...

blogs.title: Welcoming OpenShell to the CNCF: Open Governance to Secure Agentic AI
blogs.content: Posted on November 10, 2026 by Jonathan Bryce (CNCF), Ali Golshan (NVIDIA) CNCF projects highlighted in this post Today at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America, the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) welcomes OpenShell as a Sandbox project. NVIDIA has contributed OpenShell, an open source runtime for securing and governing autonomous AI agents, to the foundation’s community-led home. As organizations put AI agents to work, they need to give agents real capability without giving them unchecked access to data, secrets, or networks. This requires enforcement outside of the agents, right within the infrastructure that the agents run on. OpenShell does exactly that: it manages and monitors agent behavior, provides and enforces policy-based boundaries for what it can do. OpenShell is adopting Cedar, another CNCF project, as its policy language. It’s a great example of CNCF projects building on one another. Why this belongs in the cloud native community Agents are becoming part of cloud native infrastructure, and the layer that governs them should be shared, vendor-neutral, and open to everyone who depends on it. OpenShell already reflects that spirit. Core contributors from NVIDIA, Red Hat, Docker, and Canonical have worked on the project since its inception. Their early involvement, alongside many additional organizations adopting OpenShell shows broad industry agreement on the need for dependable controls for agentic systems. “Open source is the foundation of enterprise trust. As agents become part of cloud native infrastructure, the controls around them need to be open, auditable, and built together with the ecosystem. Bringing OpenShell to the CNCF puts governance of the project in the hands of the community. Red Hat has always believed that innovation thrives where collaboration is open, and we’re excited to help steward OpenShell alongside NVIDIA and the broader ecosystem.” — Chris Wright, Chief Technology Officer and Senior Vice President of Global Engineering, Red Hat Contributing OpenShell to the CNCF as a neutral foundation is a natural next step to expand and grow the OpenShell project. It has adopted the CNCF Code of Conduct, runs a public RFC process, and follows a governance model with explicit vendor-neutrality commitments. By contributing OpenShell alongside partners and maintainers from across the industry, NVIDIA aims to make secure AI available to all, under the same open governance model that supports other CNCF projects. Built for an ecosystem No two organizations run agents the same way. They use different infrastructure, secret stores, inference providers, and governance practices, and those choices change over time. OpenShell is designed to fit this variety through well-defined extension points for providers, compute, governance and approval workflows, policy enforcement, isolation, and credential management. Teams can adopt it incrementally and swap in what they already run. It also gives vendors, integrators, and end users clear places to contribute. What changes, and what doesn’t OpenShell is moving from NVIDIA’s GitHub repository to a neutral organization, ai-openshell. Working groups and special interest groups will form around integrated components and cross-cutting topics such as observability. The core engineering efforts from NVIDIA will continue, while we welcome contributions from other interested parties. Ways to participate Whether your organization already uses OpenShell or is just exploring it, contributing is the best way to shape its future. Areas where help is especially welcome include: Extension implementations. Reference implementations for compute, credential management, inference, and logging, along with shared documentation and conformance tests so third-party integrations behave consistently. Policy and governance patterns. Real-world approval flows, egress rules, and per-tenant policies, shared as examples or a policy library, plus feedback on the Cedar-based policy approach. Isolation and platform coverage. Broader support across Linux, macOS, and Kubernetes, security reviews, adversarial testing, and vendor-neutral confidential computing work. Observability. Consistent metrics, traces, and audit events aligned with OpenTelemetry. Packaging and release engineering. Package maintenance, reproducible builds, SBOMs, signing, and CI, all of which support Incubation requirements. Deployment at scale. Multi-tenancy, identity and access integration, and policy management workflows drawn from your own deployments. Get involved Join the community mailing list for notes and call invitations. Find the project in the CNCF Slack channel #openshell-dev . Watch the ai-openshell GitHub organization for new repositories, “good first issue” labels, and design proposals. Contributors, end users, and people who are both are welcome. We look forward to building the future of open agent governance together. Share
